content: Heel lance has traditionally been used as the standard method for obtaining blood samples in neonates for screening purposes. However, neonates undergoing heel lance experience significant pain, which cannot be entirely mitigated by current interventions. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether venepuncture is less painful and more effective than heel lance for blood sampling in term neonates. To address this, randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing the pain response to venepuncture versus heel lance were identified through a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and clinical trial registries as of May 2011. The trials included in the analysis compared the pain response to venepuncture and heel lance, with or without the use of a sweet-tasting solution as a co-intervention. Pain was assessed using validated pain measurement tools, and additional outcomes included the need for repeat sampling and cry characteristics. Statistical analyses were performed using measures such as relative risk (RR), risk difference (RD), number needed to treat (NNT), weighted mean difference (WMD), and standardized mean difference (SMD), all with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the I² statistic. Six studies involving a total of 478 neonates of varying methodological quality were included in the review. Pain was assessed in 288 neonates who did not receive a sweet-tasting solution using composite pain scales such as the Neonatal Infant Pain Scale (NIPS), Neonatal Facial Action Coding System (NFCS), and Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP). Meta-analysis revealed a significant reduction in pain scores in the venepuncture group compared to the heel lance group (SMD -0.76, 95% CI -1.00 to -0.52; I² = 0%). When a sweet-tasting solution was administered, the reduction in pain scores remained significant in favor of venepuncture (SMD -0.38, 95% CI -0.69 to -0.07). The need for repeat skin punctures was also evaluated. Four studies (n = 254) reported that venepuncture was associated with a significantly lower risk of requiring more than one skin puncture compared to heel lance (RD -0.34, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.25; I² = 97%). The number needed to treat (NNT) to avoid one repeat skin puncture was calculated to be 3 (95% CI 2 to 4). Cry characteristics, another indicator of pain, also favored the venepuncture group. However, the differences in cry characteristics between the two methods were less pronounced when a sweet-tasting solution was provided prior to the procedures. In conclusion, venepuncture, when performed by a skilled phlebotomist, appears to be the preferred method for blood sampling in term neonates due to its association with reduced pain and fewer repeat skin punctures. The administration of a sweet-tasting solution further alleviates pain during the procedure. Nonetheless, additional well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed, particularly in settings where multiple individuals with varying levels of expertise perform the procedures.
